fixes.explanation: True. "And there at Gilgal Joshua set up the twelve stones they had taken from the Jordan." (Joshua 4:20). These are the stones the twelve men carried out of the river. They came from the Jordan and now stand at Gilgal. I know a little about getting moved to a new spot, and a new place beats the back of a junk drawer every time.

I get it, it's a river, so water feels like the obvious pick. But the LORD asks for something else: twelve stones from the middle of the Jordan (Joshua 4:3). Joshua tells each man to take a stone upon his shoulder (Joshua 4:5). Good river instinct, friend, just the wrong cargo.

Traders make a fair guess, but Joshua doesn't mention any. He says the ones asking will be "your children" (Joshua 4:6). The stones are a sign among the Israelites themselves. So the question comes from inside the family.

A boundary stone marks a line, and that's a fair thought. But Joshua calls these stones a memorial to the Israelites forever (Joshua 4:7). He ties them to the waters of the Jordan being cut off before the ark. So these stones are all about what happened at the Jordan.

The city is a fair guess, but the verse sends the stones somewhere else. The Israelites carried them to the camp and set them down there (Joshua 4:8). The city isn't mentioned in that verse. Twelve stones, one camp, and I think a lot of tired shoulders.

The town of Adam isn't in this passage, so I'd skip that one, friend. Joshua sets up twelve stones in the middle of the Jordan, in the place where the priests who carried the ark of the covenant stood (Joshua 4:9). Stones in the middle of a river is a bold choice of address. Then again, I once lived in the back of a junk drawer, so I'm in no position to judge anybody's location.

Carrying the ark is the priests' job in this passage. The text speaks of "the priests who carried the ark" (Joshua 4:10), and they cross after everyone else has finished (Joshua 4:11). The Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh cross before the Israelites, armed for battle (Joshua 4:12). Different group, different job.

He exalts him. "On that day the LORD exalted Joshua in the sight of all Israel…" (Joshua 4:14). The text adds that they revered him all the days of his life. I think that's quite a day for Joshua. If somebody lifted me up like that, I'd need a taller hat.

Abraham is a big name, and I see why it came to mind. But he's not the one in this verse. It says Israel revered Joshua all the days of his life, "…just as they had revered Moses." (Joshua 4:14). Moses is the one who had directed Joshua (Joshua 4:10).

The verse goes the other way, friend. When the priests' feet touched the dry land, the waters "…returned to their course and overflowed all the banks as before." (Joshua 4:18). No heap is mentioned here. The waters come back and spill over the banks.

Shittim isn't the name in this verse. The text says the people went up from the Jordan on the tenth day of the first month and camped at Gilgal, on the eastern border of Jericho (Joshua 4:19). Gilgal is where Joshua sets up the twelve stones. That's the name to stamp in your memory, and I know a thing or two about stamping.

Dry. Joshua says to tell them, "Israel crossed the Jordan on dry ground." (Joshua 4:22). He goes on to say the LORD dried up the Jordan "…just as He did to the Red Sea…" (Joshua 4:23). Dry ground in the middle of a river, friend. I'd have checked it twice.

The text shows the kings afraid, not marching out. It says "…their hearts melted and their spirits failed for fear of the Israelites." (Joshua 5:1). No armies get gathered in this verse. What shakes them is the news of how the LORD dried up the Jordan.
